title_en: Zach Reitano - Building Ro and Why Healthcare Should Be 50% of GDP - [Invest Like the Best, EP.500]
title_zh: Ro 创始人 Zach Reitano 谈打造 Ro 与为什么医疗应占 GDP 的 50%
subtitle_zh: Zach Reitano 解析远程医疗公司 Ro 的增长逻辑，主张医疗应占 GDP 半壁江山。
summary_zh: 本期 Invest Like the Best（第 500 期）由 Patrick O'Shaughnessy 对话远程医疗公司 Ro 的创始人 Zach Reitano，核心主张颇具挑衅性：医疗未来应占 GDP 的 50% 乃至更高。Reitano 用 Jevons 悖论（Jevons paradox）论证——健康地多活一年是生活中唯一不存在边际收益递减的好东西，因此单位成本下降时市场规模反而扩大；美国医疗占 GDP 18% 之所以成问题，不在绝对数字，而在单位成本持续上行（约 50% 的开支花在 5% 的人身上）。他为美国体系「平反」：在急症护理（acute care）上，美国的癌症存活率、心梗与中风存活率高于英国 NHS 与多数 OECD 国家，且住院次数更少、时间更短，问题主要出在更高的价格与沉重的行政负担。作为 Ro 的实战者，他谈到 GLP-1 如何让肥胖率曲线首次走平、并预测十年内用药人口或超 50%（75% 的美国人超重或肥胖），以及订阅会员每年为病人省下 680 到 1,800 美元。他坚信唯一的差异化来源是持续创新、不断打上「下一个勾」（check box），并对顶尖人才（top tail）在薪酬、股权与资源上加倍投入。节目收尾落在他父亲 39 岁中风、以及「永远不要让爱停留在没说出口」的个人故事，是一集把医疗宏观叙事与创业方法论、人生体悟交织的深谈。

turns.en: I've got a first question based on our last phone call, which was something you told me which just really stood out. What percent of GDP do you think healthcare could or should be 10, 15 years from now? I think it should be as high as possible, 57. Rosary is complaining it's too high.
turns.zh: 我有一个问题，是基于我们上次通话时你跟我讲的一件事，那件事让我印象特别深刻。你觉得 10 年、15 年以后，医疗应该占 GDP 的百分之多少？——我觉得应该尽可能高，57%。Rosary 一直抱怨这个比例太高了。

turns.en: Rosary is always complaining it's too high, and I think that it's missing the force for the trees. If you think about healthcare, I think it's the cynic one on life. It's without which there is none. And it's actually depends how AI build you are, but your audience is probably pretty AI built.
turns.zh: Rosary 总是在抱怨它太高了，而我觉得这是只见树木、不见森林。如果你想想医疗，我认为它是生命中不可或缺的东西（sine qua non）——没有它，一切都不存在。这其实要看你对 AI 有多乐观（AI-bull），不过你的听众大概都相当看好 AI。

turns.en: But if you imagine a life of pure abundance, and you imagine Jevin's paradox does its thing, then the only good in our lives that does not have any diminishing larger return. Is another healthy year. And so to me, at the limit, you should be spending every single dollar towards the health of your society.
turns.zh: 但如果你想象一个纯粹丰裕的生活，再想象 Jevons 悖论（Jevons paradox）发挥作用，那么我们生活中唯一一样不存在边际收益递减的好东西，就是多健康地活一年。所以在我看来，到了极限，你应该把每一块钱都投入到社会的健康上去。

turns.en: And so when we look at the US and say, oh, we spent 18% of our GDP, that's a problem. My question is, well, why we've never used absolute numbers like that as a problem. The question is, are we getting what we want from that dollar amount?
turns.zh: 所以当我们看着美国说“哦，我们花掉了 GDP 的 18%，这是个问题”——我的疑问是，为什么？我们从来没把这种绝对数字本身当成问题。真正该问的是：我们从这笔钱里，得到我们想要的东西了吗？

turns.en: And that's the whole premise of Jevin's paradox is actually the market size increases as the cost per unit decreases. Now, the cost per unit, the challenge is in the US healthcare system, the reason why it's 18% is because the cost per unit has to rise in. We spend probably 50% of our healthcare costs on 5% of people.
turns.zh: 而这恰恰就是 Jevons 悖论的整个前提：随着单位成本下降，市场规模反而扩大。现在的问题在于单位成本——在美国医疗体系里，之所以占到 18%，是因为单位成本一直在往上走。我们大概把 50% 的医疗开支花在了 5% 的人身上。

turns.en: The US doesn't give up on a single person in that way. A lot of people look at the US healthcare system as this great anomaly relative to other healthcare systems. And I'm actually of the belief that the US healthcare system is actually a preview of what's to come for a lot of other countries.
turns.zh: 美国在这方面从不放弃任何一个人。很多人把美国医疗体系看作相对于其他医疗体系的一个巨大异类。而我其实认为，美国医疗体系恰恰是许多其他国家未来走向的一个预演。

turns.en: You look at the UK, it's GDP% of healthcare has been on GDP, went from 6 to 12. You look at Germany, went from 9 to 12. You look at the US, went from 9 to 18. And same thing with our obesity rates. And so to me, again, back to what is more important for society to spend its money on.
turns.zh: 你看英国，它的医疗占 GDP 比例从 6% 涨到了 12%；你看德国，从 9% 涨到 12%；你看美国，从 9% 涨到 18%。我们的肥胖率也是同样的情况。所以对我来说，还是回到那个问题：社会把钱花在什么上面才最重要。

turns.en: I couldn't imagine something that's more important than our health. But what we get for it should just be far greater. So if you ground us in today's reality, I'm very curious for your state of the union of the system itself. And you can picture the obesity rate chart that has, for the first time in a while,
turns.zh: 我想象不出还有什么比我们的健康更重要，但我们从中得到的回报本应远远更大。——那么，如果你把我们拉回今天的现实，我非常想听听你对这个体系本身的“国情咨文”（state of the union）式评估。你可以想象那张肥胖率曲线图——它头一回在很长一段时间里，

turns.en: and a flatlander can get the other direction. I think GOP wants the primary reason why. Obviously that's driven your business to an extraordinary degree. But give us beyond just that. Give us your sort of state of the union. Here's what health is like in the US today. Give me a little podcast by itself.
turns.zh: 开始走平、并能朝另一个方向拐。我觉得 GLP-1 是背后的首要原因，显然它在极大程度上驱动了你的业务。但除了这一点之外，也给我们讲讲——给我们你的那份“国情咨文”：今天的美国医疗到底是什么样，就当是你自己的一个小播客。

turns.en: It's interesting to think about first, where does it money go? Usually if you want to understand the industry, you just follow the money. So let's say 30 to 35% is about hospital systems. 20 to 25% might be doctor's office. Another 9 to 10% would be drugs and pharmaceuticals. And then you see the remainder chopped up there.
turns.zh: 有意思的是先想想：钱都流到哪儿去了？通常你想理解一个行业，只要跟着钱走就行。大概 30% 到 35% 是医院系统，20% 到 25% 可能是医生诊所，另有 9% 到 10% 是药品和制药，剩下的则被切碎分摊在各处。

turns.en: And then a lot of people will talk about and back to our question a little bit around percentage EEP. The US health care system, I would say, is really fantastic. Better than people give it credit for at acute care. Yes, it's more expensive. But we have higher cancer survival rates than the NHS.
turns.zh: 然后很多人会谈到——回到我们关于占 GDP 百分比的那个问题——我会说，美国医疗体系其实相当出色，比人们给它的评价要好，尤其是在急症护理（acute care）方面。是的，它更贵，但我们的癌症存活率高于英国 NHS。

turns.en: If you have a heart attack or stroke, you want to have it in the US. Our survival rates are higher on average than other OECD countries. And we don't use more health care than other OECD countries. We have fewer hospital stays. Our hospital stays are shorter.
turns.zh: 如果你要犯心脏病或中风，你会希望它发生在美国。我们的平均存活率高于其他 OECD 国家。而且我们用的医疗资源并不比其他 OECD 国家多：我们住院次数更少，住院时间更短。

turns.en: We have slightly more procedures and scans, which whereas it nets out on a per unit basis, and our prices are higher, and our administrative burden is much, much, much higher. And then a lot of people will talk about life expectancy in the US. It has an increase in the last 10, 15 years.
turns.zh: 我们做的操作和扫描稍微多一些，但按单位算下来其实相抵；而我们的价格更高，行政负担则要高得多、多得多、多得多。然后很多人会谈到美国的预期寿命，它在过去 10 到 15 年里其实是上升的。

turns.en: But to me, a lot of that is not a reflection of our health care system. So there's kind of two buckets of the way we die. The first is like this fast clock. And that will bring down the average of the US. Like the pregnancy relative to other OECD countries.
turns.zh: 但在我看来，这在很大程度上并不能反映我们的医疗体系。所以我们死的方式大致分两个桶。第一个是那种“快时钟”（fast clock），它会拉低美国的平均值，比如相对于其他 OECD 国家的妊娠相关问题。

turns.en: So that fast clock is like, gun deaths, car accidents, overdoses, things like that. That will bring down an average. But it's not the majority of the way we die. The majority of the way we die is at a slow clock, right? Chronic disease. And that has massively been rising. As you mentioned in the last 20, 30, 40 years ago.
turns.zh: 所以那个“快时钟”指的是枪支死亡、车祸、药物过量之类的东西，它会拉低平均值，但它并不是我们死亡的主要方式。我们死亡的主要方式是“慢时钟”（slow clock），也就是慢性病，而正如你提到的，在过去 20、30、40 年里，慢性病一直在大幅上升。

turns.en: So those two things are really the makeup of how illness happens in the US and how people die. And then that's how the money yet spent. Is he thinking about the whole thing? What is the most surprising thing that you've come to learn about the system that you think people may not appreciate fully?
turns.zh: 所以这两样东西真正构成了美国疾病如何发生、人们如何死亡的图景，钱也就是这么花掉的。——他是在想整个体系吗？关于这个体系，你了解到的、最让你意外、觉得人们可能没有充分意识到的一点是什么？

turns.en: There's probably two things that I would say. One is I do think our health care system has one, if not two, but one central flaw, from which all other problems stem. And the second is that the entire health care system is based on time horizons that are almost irrelevant to the individual.
turns.zh: 我想大概有两点。第一，我确实认为我们的医疗体系有一个（如果不是两个，那就是一个）核心缺陷，所有其他问题都由此派生。第二，整个医疗体系所基于的时间跨度，对个人而言几乎毫无意义。

turns.en: So that's what I think of the surprising thing, which is when you go into the health care system, there's a fundamental mismatch of incentives. And if I had to say, what is the problem with our health care system? It is that the patient is not the customer. That's the problem that we're trying to solve at Ro.
turns.zh: 所以这就是我觉得意外的地方：当你走进医疗体系，会发现激励存在根本性的错配。如果非要我说出我们医疗体系的问题是什么，那就是——病人并不是客户。这正是我们在 Ro 试图解决的问题。

turns.en: And I think you see it working, but that is the fundamental problem. And the reason being is, I mean, you see this in every business that you talk to. Whoever controls the flow of money at the point of purchase, that's the customer. That's the stakeholder that everyone builds around. And patients, individuals, we pay for our health care.
turns.zh: 而且我觉得你能看到它在奏效，但这才是那个根本问题。原因在于——我是说，你在跟他聊的每一家企业里都能看到这一点：谁在购买发生的那一刻掌控钱的流向，谁就是客户，就是所有人围绕其构建产品的那个利益相关方。而我们病人、个人，是为自己的医疗付钱的，

turns.en: We just are not the customer in the majority of the air actions. So our out of pocket expenses and minority of our expenses. And we pay through our taxes and we play through suppressed wages with our employer. And so you then look and say, okay, well, where's health care working? Where does it feel really good?
turns.zh: 只是在大多数互动里，我们并不是那个客户。所以我们的自付费用（out-of-pocket）只占我们开支的一小部分，我们是通过税收付钱、通过被压低的工资（配合雇主）付钱。于是你就会去看：好，那医疗在哪儿是奏效的？在哪儿让人感觉特别好？

turns.en: And it feels really good where it's cash pay. Where the patient is the customer. It's a favorite example of that. You look at laced eye surgery. Cost comes down, quality improves, convenience improves. You look at breast augmentation. You look at cosmetic surgeries. Cost comes down, quality improves, convenience improves.
turns.zh: 而让人感觉特别好的地方，恰恰是现金支付（cash pay）的地方，是病人即客户的地方。我最喜欢的一个例子就是激光眼科手术（LASIK）：成本下降、质量提升、便利性提升。再看隆胸、整形手术：成本下降、质量提升、便利性提升。

turns.en: You look at GLP ones. I take GLP ones and they are like this beautiful foil for the rest of the health care system. Politicians and regulators have been trying to get transparent prices for 20, 25 years. What happens? Farma goes direct. What happens to the prices?
turns.zh: 再看 GLP-1。我自己就在用 GLP-1，它们就像整个医疗体系的一面绝妙的镜子。政客和监管者花了 20、25 年想搞出透明价格，结果呢？药企直接面向消费者（direct-to-consumer）。价格会怎样？

turns.en: Well, this as my loving Jewish mother would say, the Fakokta prices of Listene. You have $1,300 drugs that people are paying behind the scenes, $3, $400 for. What happens when those go direct to consumer? That Listeneck act gets entirely limited.
turns.zh: 嗯，用我那位可爱的犹太妈妈的话说，那标价（list price）真是乱成一团。有些药标价 1,300 美元，而人们在幕后其实只花 300、400 美元。当这些药直接面向消费者时会怎样？那个标价体系就被彻底打破了。

turns.en: When people are pointing fingers between insurance companies and PBMs and Farman, who's to blame? They go direct. You remove the PBM and insurance company entirely. And normally branded drugs every year systematically. They go at 6, 7, 8%, year-rear-rear. And so the patent cliff, my hope, and I think you're already starting to see this,
turns.zh: 当人们在保险公司、PBM（药品福利管理机构，pharmacy benefit manager）和药企之间互相指责、追问该怪谁时，他们就直接面向消费者了：你把 PBM 和保险公司整个移除掉。而通常那些品牌药每年都在系统性地涨价，一年年地涨 6%、7%、8%。所以专利悬崖（patent cliff）——我的希望，而且我觉得你已经开始看到，

turns.en: more middlemen that do absolutely nothing are getting removed from the process. So they are able to capture the same, if not more gross profit, while prices come down. If you look at lilies earnings, prices come down, volume far outstrips it. And PBMs, to me, they are like the appendix of the health care system.
turns.zh: 越来越多什么都不干的中间人被从流程里移除掉。于是他们能够攫取同样多、甚至更多的毛利，同时价格却在下降。如果你看礼来（Lilly）的财报，价格下降，但销量的增长远远盖过了它。而 PBM 在我看来，就像医疗体系的阑尾。

turns.en: At one point in time, they might have served some purpose, but it was so long ago that people can't remember what that was. And turns out when you remove them from the equation, software can do exactly what they would have done historically. And so you even see what you'll be wanting. PBM goes away. Insurance company largely goes away.
turns.zh: 在某个历史时点它们也许起过某种作用，但那已是久远到大家都不记得那作用是什么了。而事实证明，当你把它们从这个等式里拿掉，软件完全能做它们过去做的那些事。所以你甚至能看到——你肯定会想看到——PBM 消失，保险公司在很大程度上也消失。

turns.en: People can debate that and whether or not it should and what they should cover. But for cash pay purposes, PBMs and insurance companies go away. Prices go from $1,300 to $149. And the people making the drugs are making more money. And so you can see that where it's working, the patient is in control at the center.
turns.zh: 人们可以就此争论，讨论它该不该消失、该覆盖什么。但就现金支付而言，PBM 和保险公司会消失，价格从 1,300 美元降到 149 美元，而造药的人反而赚得更多。所以你能看到：在奏效的地方，是病人在中心掌握了主导权。

turns.en: And then you usually have people give this criticism. One of the most common is asymmetry of information. And in my mind, it's a little bit similar like the best form of government. So democracy is the worst form of government, except for all the other ones.
turns.zh: 然后通常有人会提出这样的批评，最常见的一种是信息不对称（asymmetry of information）。而在我看来，这有点类似于“最好的政府形式”那个说法：民主是最糟糕的政府形式，除了其他所有那些之外。

turns.en: In my mind, the patient is the worst person to own their health care decisions, except for literally everyone else. And when you go into our health care system today, they'll say there's asymmetry of information. You have to sign on the dotted line away and everything. And you're not reading that.
turns.zh: 在我看来，病人是掌控自己医疗决策的最糟糕人选，除了字面意义上的所有其他人之外。而当你今天走进我们的医疗体系，他们会说存在信息不对称，你得在虚线上签字、把一切都让渡出去，而你根本没在读那些内容。

turns.en: But imagine you had recourse, which is, get to vote with your feet. So if hypothetically, when we, as a society, well, sometimes you have the price transparency loss for hospitals. And people thought that that was this amazing thing. That is epic lipstick on a pig. No industry could survive with its prices not being public.
turns.zh: 但想象一下你有追索权，也就是能用脚投票。所以假想一下，当我们作为一个社会——嗯，有时候你会有医院的价格透明法，人们以为那是件了不起的事。那其实不过是在猪身上涂口红、纯粹自欺欺人。没有任何一个行业能在价格不公开的情况下存活。

turns.en: Any company that did that wouldn't get any customers. turns.zh: 而我很幸运。我从小和我爸一起长大，他是一名医生，他救过我的命。我 18 岁时有一个心脏方面的基础问题、做了一次心脏手术。但他帮助我实现了健康目标，好让我去追求人生目标，所以他帮我走过了 18 岁时的那次手术。

turns.zh: 而那时我本来就很矮小、经常被欺负。我父母和医疗体系抗争，想让它报销、帮我拿到生长激素。所以有大约六年时间，我每天都往腿上打一针。于是我进高中时大概 4 英尺 8、9 英寸，出来时变成了 6 英尺 1 英寸。

turns.zh: 所以如果你想从我自己的角度去体会这几条不同的路径：本来可能有一天我 18 岁时还是 5 英尺 3、还伴着勃起功能障碍——这实在不太妙；或者，长到 6 英尺 1，并且和这个世界上最了不起的人结了婚。

turns.en: And I do think that it was because my parents and my dad were constantly fighting with the healthcare system. They set me on an entirely different trajectory as an individual. On the societal impact, whenever we as a society, whenever we attack the leading causes of death, just upstream, not downstream, but upstream when we attack those,
turns.zh: 而我确实认为，这是因为我父母、我爸一直在和医疗体系抗争，他们把我这个个体放到了一条完全不同的轨迹上。说到社会层面的影响：每当我们作为一个社会去攻克那些主要死因——不是在下游，而是在上游攻克它们时，

turns.en: you see the shape of society dramatically shift on the other side. So from year zero to 1800, our life expectancy is 30. And a lot of people will say, yeah, it's infant mortality. Like, yes, it was infant mortality. It's also maternal mortality. It's also infectious disease. It was big free.
turns.zh: 你就会看到社会形态在另一侧发生剧烈转变。所以从公元零年到 1800 年，我们的预期寿命是 30 岁。很多人会说，那是婴儿死亡率的问题。是的，是婴儿死亡率，但也是产妇死亡率，也是传染病在作祟。

turns.en: What ends up happening when we largely combat infectious disease and infant mortality and maternal mortality? They're no longer mourning the loss of children and spouses every single day. They invest in the kids that they have. Those kids go to high school. They go to college, women enter the workforce. We have the industrial revolution.
turns.zh: 当我们大体上战胜了传染病、婴儿死亡率和产妇死亡率之后，会发生什么？他们不再每天为孩子和配偶的离世而哀恸，就会把资源投入到已有的孩子身上。这些孩子上高中、上大学，女性进入职场，我们迎来工业革命。

turns.en: 40% of the population goes from making food to four. We get electricity from 10% of pounds to 100%. And all of that happened, I believe, because health is a precondition to progress. And so right now, if we think of the leading causes of death as the thing I just mentioned, those chronic diseases, if we can attack those upstream,
turns.zh: 40% 的人口从“务农生产食物”中解放出来；我们的电力普及率从 10% 提升到 100%。而我相信，所有这一切之所以发生，是因为健康是进步的先决条件。所以此刻，如果我们把主要死因——也就是我刚提到的那些慢性病——当作目标，如果我们能在上游攻克它们，

turns.en: I think we can shift the trajectory of our society in ways that we cannot predict, in ways that will be beautiful and amazing and can't wait to see what happens. Do you think that if you had to predict the percent of people on some form of a GLP1 10 years from now or something, will your prediction be from 10 or 15 to that?

turns.en: 50 plus percent of people. Do you think it'll just be a standard, whether or not you have the acute versions of the things that were originally on that label? Yeah, absolutely. What's interesting to me is if you think about it, so just pure raw numbers. 75% of the US population has overweight or has obesity.
turns.zh: 会变成 50% 以上的人吗？你觉得它会成为一种常态吗——无论你有没有那些最初适应症标签上所列病症的急性版本？——当然会。有意思的是，如果你想想，光是纯粹的数字：75% 的美国人口超重或肥胖。

turns.en: So just based on that, that group is going to get eligible. And then we say, okay, well, that flottens up. And what about top down? What percentage of the US population is metabolically healthy? 10 to 12%. So they're even interested in taking it prophylactically for inflammation or geroprotective reasons.
turns.zh: 所以单凭这一点，这个群体就会变得符合用药条件。然后我们会说，好，那条曲线走平了，那自上而下看呢？有多大比例的美国人是代谢健康的？只有 10% 到 12%。所以，如果他们甚至有兴趣为了抗炎或“老年保护”（geroprotective）的原因而预防性地用药——

turns.en: So he starts sitting here and say, of course, there are some people who should not be on this medication or they might not be able to tolerate it. But as we improve the tolerability, and I was we better understand a lot of their mechanisms of action,
turns.zh: 所以你会坐在这儿说：当然，有一些人不应该用这种药，或者可能无法耐受它。但随着我们改善耐受性、随着我们更好地理解它们的很多作用机制，

turns.en: I think what we are seeing is it combats a lot of the environmental and genetic impacts that lead to chronic disease in society today. And then there's obviously the massive affordability question. But to me, hey, I think the majority of people will be on it. I think statins are a good comp. You see 40, 50 million people on it.
turns.zh: 我认为我们正在看到的，是它能够对抗当今社会里导致慢性病的很多环境和遗传因素。然后显然还有一个巨大的可负担性问题。但对我来说，嘿，我认为大多数人都会用上它。我觉得他汀类药物（statins）是个很好的对照：你会看到四五千万人在用它。

turns.en: And these are much more effective, just a breathable label. Before we close out this chapter of the state of the union and the system, I love this notion of jobs over lives as one framework. Talk to us about what you're thinking here. Yeah, so there's one of those that might be a little bit more controversial, but we can do it.
turns.zh: 而它们的效果要好得多，适应症范围也更广。在我们结束这一章“国情咨文”式的体系评估之前，我很喜欢“要饭碗还是要命”（jobs over lives）这个框架。跟我们讲讲你在这方面的思考吧。——是的，这个话题可能会有点争议，但我们可以聊。

turns.en: There's a conversation in health care that's happening right now. I don't think you see it in other industries where people say things like health care must remain human. And I think it's the entire wrong question to ask ourselves. Not that I don't think parts of it will, but it's an obsession over inputs instead of outcomes.
turns.zh: 眼下医疗领域正在进行一场对话——我觉得你在别的行业看不到——人们会说类似“医疗必须保持由人来做”这样的话。而我认为，这是在问自己一个完全错误的问题。倒不是说我觉得其中一部分不会由人来做，但这是在痴迷于投入（inputs），而不是结果（outcomes）。

turns.en: And I think that when you do that, you are not prioritizing patient health outcomes about everything else. And so I think tools, both humans and new technology, must earn their place. And the status quo does not get a pass just because it's of its current existence.
turns.zh: 我认为，当你那样做时，你就没有把病人的健康结果置于其他一切之上。所以我觉得，无论是人还是新技术这样的工具，都必须靠自己去赢得一席之地，而现状并不能仅仅因为它当前存在，就自动获得豁免。

turns.en: And so I think driverless cars are a great example in my mind where we are having quite a bizarre conversation in my opinion, which is about 40,000 people a year die from car accidents. That is almost the same exact numbers that people who die from breast cancer every single year, nuts, absolutely nuts.
turns.zh: 所以在我看来，无人驾驶汽车是个很好的例子。我认为我们正在进行的是一场相当古怪的对话：每年大约有 4 万人死于车祸，这个数字几乎和每年死于乳腺癌的人数一模一样，太离谱了，简直离谱。

turns.en: Driverless cars in pockets have proven to be 10, 20 times safer than a human drug. So we basically, for certain types of cancer, have a cure. And the conversation is not, how do we have operation warp speed for this cure for cancer? It is a lot about and more about job displacement. And it's not that I want to diminish job displacement.
turns.zh: 在某些区域里，无人驾驶汽车已被证明比人类驾驶安全 10 倍、20 倍。所以基本上，对某些类型的癌症我们已经有了“解药”。可对话的主题却不是“我们该如何为这个癌症解药搞一场‘曲速行动’（Operation Warp Speed）”，而更多是关于岗位流失。倒不是说我想淡化岗位流失的问题，

turns.en: It's that we should not, we should not and we cannot prioritize jobs over lots. If we were talking about a cure for cancer and someone said, what about the people currently treating cancer patients without the cure? I don't even know that they would be able to add to the stupidest idea ever.
turns.zh: 而是说，我们不应该、也绝不能把“饭碗”置于“性命”之上。如果我们在谈一个癌症的解药，而有人说“那现在那些没有解药、正在治疗癌症病人的人怎么办？”——我甚至不知道他们怎么好意思说出口，这是有史以来最愚蠢的想法。

turns.en: There's a story that I heard a CEO of a driverless car company say they were speaking to a regulator. And the regulator asked the CEO when they told them about the reduction of deaths. The regulator said, but what about the organs? And the CEO was flabbergasted.
turns.zh: 有个故事，是我听一家无人驾驶汽车公司的 CEO 讲的：他们在跟一位监管者交谈。当 CEO 告诉对方死亡人数会减少时，这位监管者问：“那器官怎么办？”CEO 当时就惊呆了。

turns.en: What the regulator was referring to is the organs from people who are dying in car accidents. I can save other people's lives. A beautiful thing, having said that, what the CEO's response was, I don't know what they said about loud,
turns.zh: 监管者所指的，是那些在车祸中死去的人的器官——它们能救其他人的命，这是件美好的事。话虽如此，CEO 的回应是——我不知道他们大声说了什么，

turns.en: but at least when they told me this about the had in their head, was hopefully they're still in the original person. And so I think that we as a society, especially when it comes to health, must prioritize outcomes over inputs. The new thing must prove its worth.
turns.zh: 但至少当他们把这个故事讲给我听时，他们脑子里想的是：“但愿那些器官还留在原来那个人身上。”所以我认为，作为一个社会，尤其是在健康这件事上，我们必须把结果置于投入之上。新事物必须证明自己的价值。

turns.en: So it's not that, hey, technology automatically gets a free pass. It doesn't. It must prove, not that it's 1% better, but that is substantially better than the status quo. But we, as a result, cannot get the status quo a pass. And I think we see that with driverless cars right now. And it's a very painful conversation.
turns.zh: 所以并不是说，嘿，技术就自动拿到免检金牌，它没有。它必须证明——不是只比现状好 1%，而是实质性地优于现状。但反过来，我们也不能因为现状是现状就给它开脱。我觉得我们现在在无人驾驶汽车上就能看到这一点，而那是一场非常痛苦的对话。

turns.en: And I do believe that the people impeding driverless cars where they're proven to be safe should have a body count attached to their name. Truly. And I think we will look back on it as such. And I think that one of my biggest worries is related to health care, that we will have that same level of prioritizing inputs over outcomes.
turns.zh: 我确实认为，那些在无人驾驶汽车已被证明安全的地方仍然加以阻挠的人，名字后面应该附一个“死亡人数”。说真的。我认为我们日后回望时也会这么看。而我觉得我最大的担忧之一就和医疗有关：我们会在“把投入置于结果之上”这件事上犯同样严重的错误。

turns.en: Now mind you 11 months prior in January we had raised $500 million to $5 billion valuation. And we did almost every textbook mistake in the book. We confused our long term vision with our near term strategy and we decided to do everything and hire everyone and try to do everything all at once. And that was a disaster.
turns.zh: 要知道，在那之前 11 个月，也就是 1 月，我们刚以 50 亿美元估值融了 5 亿美元。而我们几乎把教科书上的每一个错误都犯了个遍：我们把长期愿景和近期战略混为一谈，决定什么都做、什么人都招、想一口气把所有事都做了。那是一场灾难。

turns.en: And I realized that people like how did you not realize that? turns.zh: 我意识到——人们会想“你怎么会没看出来？”。当一切顺风顺水时，你有时看着季度业绩、年度业绩，或者在某个适合反思的好时机，它才像一吨砖头一样把我砸醒。所以我在飞机上盯着这些数据：我们 2021 年只增长了 9%，账上有好几亿美元，

turns.en: And we were burning but we were what I would call a zombie company which is like you're not growing fast enough to get out of it but you're not burning where you're going to die.
